paragraphs: Even if I granted everything I have been refuting, the friends of despotism would be no better off. There will always be a great difference between subduing a multitude and ruling a society. Suppose scattered individuals were enslaved one after another by a single man, however many they might be. I still see only a master and his slaves, certainly not a people and its ruler. I see what might be called an aggregation, but not an association; there is as yet neither public good nor body politic. That man, even if he has enslaved half the world, is still only an individual; his interest, separate from that of others, is still a purely private interest. If this same man dies, his empire after him remains scattered and without unity, just as an oak falls apart and dissolves into a heap of ashes once fire has consumed it.

A people, says Grotius, can give itself to a king. Then, according to Grotius, a people is already a people before it gives itself. The gift is itself a civil act, and it requires public deliberation. Before examining the act by which a people gives itself to a king, it would be better to examine the act by which it became a people. That act necessarily comes first, and it is the true foundation of society.

Indeed, if there were no earlier convention, where would the minority’s obligation to accept the majority’s choice come from, unless the election were unanimous? What right have a hundred men who want a master to vote on behalf of ten who do not? The rule of majority voting is itself established by convention, and it presupposes unanimity on at least one occasion.
